column28: Few fish remains were recovered but over 2,000 marine mollusk shells were found at the site. Étienne et al. (1994) felt this site could not be securely identified as a fish-salting workshop but subsequent authors were slightly more optimistic. Most recently, Teichner (2005; 2006; 2007; 2008b, 562–570; 2008a) has identified these vats as part of a facility for making purple dye from murex snails. His identification is plausible, but I have chosen to include the vats in this data set to avoid prejudicing my analysis. His identification was based partly on a contrast between the isolated nature of these vats and the batteries found in a selective list of larger fish-salting facilities, but I have accepted other solitary and scattered vats into my set of possible salting workshops; he also cited the large numbers of murex shells found at the site, but such material also has been found at accepted salting facilities with many adjoining vats. Therefore, a priori it is not clear how reliable either criterion is as an indicator of dye-related activities; moreover, his identification of the salting vats in Area A provides reasonable doubt regarding the purpose of those in Area J. The results of this study, however, endorse a more skeptical approach to these "salting" vats in the future, thereby lending support to Teichner's final interpretation, if not to the details of his justification.

column57: Over a hundred so-called fish-salting vats have been reported at the site; fish remains were found at the bottom of some (Romančuk 2005, 104). Few vats have been published in any detail and the features would benefit from a careful re-examination. The vat numbering employed here was adopted from Romančuk (1977), who published a table with basic identifying and descriptive information about many of the vats. The "Agoranomos Inscription" (see Semenov-Zuser 1947) has often been cited in support of an important fish salting industry at Chersonesos, but a recent review questions this conclusion (Bekker-Nielsen 2007). The scholarship cited below in the site bibliography speaks to fish-salting at the site generally. References to specific groups of vats can be found under their respective workshop entries.

column19: When the vat was built in the 1st–2nd centuries CE, it was paved with a layer of thin tiles covered with mortar and the walls were coated with an unknown type of plaster. In the 5th–6th centuries CE it was repaved with bricks covered in mortar. This vat has been entered twice in order to allow the second lining to appear in statistical analyses of construction materials; in all other statistics, only the first phase has been counted.

column19: The site is located near the former building of the Guardia Civil and near the "Castillo de la Duquesa"; both structures have lent their names to the facility. The site has not been fully published. The RAMPPA entry reports that there were at least 30 vats around the central courtyard (see also García Vargas and Bernal Casasola 2009, 154). It appears to me, however, that there are two courtyards of vats. The eastern courtyard has vats lining its northern and western sides, forming an L-shape (vats 1–19). Along the eastern side of vats 1–15 are a number of pillars that look like the roof supports that often are found in fish-salting workshops (e.g., Baelo Claudia/Bolonia, Conjunto Industrial XII; Metrouna; Torre García; Torremolinos, La Cizaña; Tróia, Workshops 1 and 2). The western wall of vats 1–15 also looks thicker, suggesting that it supported a full, load-bearing wall. Both of these facts indicate that the long line of vats 1–15 belong to this eastern courtyard rather than the central courtyard. This leaves the central courtyard with just one row of vats (20–36) on its western side. I suspect that both courtyards belonged to the same owner, though, so I do not believe it is necessary to divide them into two workshops. A Roman villa is located just west of the complex.

column28: Previous critiques of this identification were based on a supposed lack of fish remains, although their presence was noted in the initial publication of the vats (Ellis 2011, 68; cf. Botte 2015, 685; Monteix 2016c, 221). Subsequent study of the environmental remains from the site has confirmed that several vats did, in fact, contain a high concentration of marine remains, and they were even more abundant in the soak-aways that seem to have been used alongside them to dispose of processing waste (see Chapter 4, sub-section 4.3.2.4; Ellis et al., forthcoming; Motz, forthcoming[b]). Moreover, many other installations that have been confidently identified as fish-salting workshops did not contain vats with large amounts of fish remains, including some that were positively identified by the same scholars (Guéthary; Camargue: Carrelet; Marina di Pulsano; Santa Irene; Favignana; Isola delle Femmine; Lampedusa; Pachino; San Vito lo Capo; Vendicari; Giannutri; Giglio), in one case incorrectly (Portus Fenilie/Tombolo di Feniglia; see Appendix E), or were even excavated by them (Levanzo). Other notable examples with a confirmed lack of fish bones or scales include Workshop 12 at Tróia, while countless others contained only a handful of remains.

column19: The workshop includes 27 rectangular vats and 26 circular vats (note that the vat numbering is taken from the published plans, which only show circular vats 3–28; it is unclear whether circular vats 1–2 never existed or existed but were not shown). The vats are located in three main areas: the western area contains 24 circular vats and 11 rectangular vats; the central area contains two circular vats and at least six rectangular vats; the eastern area contains at least 10 rectangular vats. The ceramic evidence attests to a long occupation at the site: the earliest materials date from the 5th century BCE; the workshop was abandoned in the 3rd or 4th century CE and a house was built on top of some vats. An absolute chronology within this span of time cannot be determined from the directly datable materials. Botte, however, argues for four phases of construction in and around the workshop (Botte 2009, 171; 2016, 240). First, the circular vats 15–25 were built in the first half of the 4th century BCE. Some time afterward, circular vats 3–8 and 26–28 were added. In the 3rd century BCE, a building with an oven was constructed. Finally, the rectangular vats were installed in the Augustan period or the 1st century CE. This proposed chronology is based almost entirely on form.

column57: Nearly all of the vats are located in the Parque Botánico El Majuelo. The remains can only be viewed from the perimeter. CONFIGURATION: In grouping the vats into workshops, I have followed the divisions listed by Étienne and Mayet (2002, 100). South of the workshops there are rooms for storage, preparation, and/or administration. One of these rooms contained a reused stone pedestal with an inscription (ILPG 8); it has been proposed that the individuals mentioned in it were involved in fish salting, but I argue against this interpretation (see discussion in Chapter 4, section 4.1.4). PLAN: The site has not been fully published and no comprehensive plan seems to exist (see the comment by Étienne and Mayet 2002, 97). Therefore, I have produced my own plan by combining satellite imagery with the few early plans that showed the peripheral areas, along with a 3D photogrammetric model of the central area produced from photographs taken during my visit to the site. DATING: The earliest activity at the site dates to the Punic period (late 5th to early 4th century BCE); some material from the 1st century BCE was found in the same sounding (Molina Fajardo et al. 1984). No workshops from these early phases, however, have been identified. The excavated workshops were active from the 1st century CE to the late 4th/early 5th century (Molina Fajardo and Jiménez Contreras 1984). This important site would benefit from a full cleaning and re-evaluation of its architectural stratigraphy in order to refine our understanding of the property divisions and sequence of construction, as well as selective soundings to provide a more precise absolute chronology. The production of a more formal, detailed plan would also be a welcome contribution. BIBLIOGRAPHY: The bibliography listed below covers the entire site, but especially Workshops 1–9 and the vats entered under Other Workshops. More specific citations have been listed under the entries for the other four groups of vats.

column19: The facility has a moderately complex chronology. The first iteration of the workshop with vats 1–19 was built in the 1st—2nd centuries CE (Vaz Pinto et al. 2011). At this time, Workshops 1 and 2 were a single factory with two production units connected by a corridor. The well north of the workshop was built in the 2nd century CE (Vaz Pinto et al. 2010b). In the second phase (first quarter of the 3rd century—first half of the 4th century), the workshop was separated from Workshop 2, vats 31–33 were added, and it was subdivided into three parts: 1A, 1B and 1C (Vaz Pinto et al. 2014a). In the third phase (first half of the 4th century—second quarter of the 5th century CE; Vaz Pinto et al. 2012), workshop 1B was attached to workshop 2; in workshops 1A and 1C, vats 8–10, 12, and 17 were subdivided (Vaz Pinto et al. 2014a).
